ruwiki-junker-rising.cite: Russian Wikipedia, “Восстание юнкеров в Петрограде” (the rising of the yunkers in Petrograd), read 2026-11-02.

factions.name: Monarchists and Octobrists
factions.sum: The old right. In Reed’s ten days they no longer act in their own name; their men work through the Cadets and the generals.

def.q: These once-powerful factions no longer existed openly; they either worked underground, or their members joined the Cadets, as the Cadets came by degrees to stand for their political programme.

bg.en: The Octobrists, the Union of 17 October, took their name from the Tsar’s manifesto of October 1905 that promised a constitution, and were the largest party of the Third Duma. Mikhail Rodzianko, an Octobrist, chaired the Duma from 1911 until 1917; Vasily Shulgin led the Duma’s Russian nationalists. After the February Revolution the monarchist right lost its place in open politics.

factions.name: Cadets (Constitutional Democrats)
factions.sum: The liberal party of the propertied and the professions: its men sit in the last Kerensky cabinet, the Council of the Republic and the City Duma, and fight the rising from them.

def.q: So-called from the initials of its name, Constitutional Democrats. Its official name is “Party of the People’s Freedom.”

also.q: As the Revolution became more and more a social economic Revolution, the Cadets grew more and more conservative.

bg.en: Founded in 1905 and led by the historian Pavel Miliukov, the party of liberal lawyers, professors and zemstvo men stood for a constitutional state, civil rights and, in 1917, a republic that would fight the war to victory. Its leaders formed most of the first Provisional Government. On 11 December 1917 the Soviet government declared it a party of “enemies of the people” and arrested its leaders.

factions.name: Group of Public Men
factions.sum: Moscow’s bankers and manufacturers: their delegates hold portfolios in Kerensky’s last cabinet, Konovalov among them.

def.q: After the Cadets had become unpopular through their relations with the Kornilov counter-revolution, the Group of Public Men was formed in Moscow.

also.q: It was composed of the more “modern” bankers, merchants and manufacturers, who were intelligent enough to realise that the Soviets must be fought by their own weapon—economic organisation.

bg.en: The Conference of Public Figures met in Moscow in August 1917, on the eve of General Kornilov’s attempt on Petrograd, with Mikhail Rodzianko in the chair; it brought together industrialists, bankers, landowners and conservative politicians who wanted a strong government against the Soviets. Alexander Konovalov, a textile magnate, was deputy prime minister in Kerensky’s last cabinet.

factions.name: Populist Socialists (Trudoviki)
factions.sum: A small, cautious socialist party of the cooperatives; it stands with the Government and the Duma against the rising.

def.q: Numerically a small party, composed of cautious intellectuals, the leaders of the Cooperative societies, and conservative peasants.

also.q: Kerensky was the leader of the Trudoviki in the Imperial Duma when the Revolution of March, 1917, broke out.

bg.en: The Popular Socialists broke away from the Socialist Revolutionaries’ right in 1906, rejecting terror and the immediate socialisation of the land; in June 1917 they merged with the Trudoviks, the peasant Labour Group of the Imperial Duma, as the Labour Popular Socialist Party. Aleksey Peshekhonov was minister of food in 1917, and Nikolai Tchaikovsky, a veteran of the 1870s, led the Cooperative movement.

factions.name: Russian Social Democratic Labour Party
factions.sum: Russia’s Marxist party, long split: by 1917 its wings, from the Bolsheviki to Plekhanov’s Yedinstvo, are parties of their own, on both sides of the barricades.

def.q: At a party congress held in 1903, the party split, on the question of tactics, into two factions—the Majority (Bolshinstvo), and the Minority (Menshinstvo).

also.q: These two wings became two separate parties, both calling themselves “Russian Social Democratic Labour Party,” and both professing to be Marxians.

bg.en: Founded at Minsk in 1898. At its Second Congress, in Brussels and London in 1903, Lenin’s followers and Martov’s split over who should be a member of the party: Lenin wanted a tight body of professional revolutionaries, Martov a broader party. The two wings, Bolsheviks and Mensheviks, were separate parties by 1912.

factions.name: Mensheviki (Mensheviks)
factions.sum: The moderate Marxists, in coalition with the Cadets since May; they walk out of the Congress of Soviets and join the Committee for Salvation.

def.q: This party includes all shades of Socialists who believe that society must progress by natural evolution toward Socialism, and that the working-class must conquer political power first.

also.q: This was the party of the Socialist intellectuals

bg.en: The Mensheviks held that backward Russia was ready only for a bourgeois, democratic revolution, which the workers should push forward but not lead to socialism at once. In 1917 the “defencists” among them, led by Irakli Tsereteli, Fyodor Dan and Nikolay Chkheidze, dominated the Soviets until September, entered the coalition government in May and backed the defence of the country in the war.

pic.t: Tcheidze, Tseretelli, Kameniev, Avksentiev and Schreider
pic.lic: Public domain: printed in Reed’s Ten Days That Shook the World (New York: Boni and Liveright, 1919) (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-1923}})
pic.cap: From the left, Tcheidze, Tseretelli, Kameniev, Avksentiev and Schreider: a plate in Reed’s 1919 edition. Tcheidze presided over the old Tsay-ee-kah and Tseretelli led the Mensheviki in the Soviets; Kameniev presided over the Second Congress; Avksentiev was president of the Peasants’ Soviets, and Schreider Mayor of Petrograd.

factions.name: Menshevik Internationalists
factions.sum: Martov’s left Mensheviks: against the war and the coalition, and against the rising too; they leave the Congress, then work for a government of all the socialist parties.

def.q: The radical wing of the Mensheviki, internationalists and opposed to all coalition with the propertied classes; yet unwilling to break loose from the conservative Mensheviki, and opposed to the dictatorship of the working-class advocated by the Bolsheviki.

also.q: Trotzky was long a member of this group.

bg.en: Martov’s internationalists opposed the war from 1914 and the coalition with the Cadets in 1917. At the opening of the Second Congress of Soviets Martov proposed a peaceful settlement and a government of all the socialist parties; when the Congress endorsed the rising he walked out, and Trotsky told him to go where he belonged, into the dustbin of history.

factions.name: Bolsheviki (Bolsheviks)
factions.sum: Lenin’s party, with the majority in the Petrograd Soviet: it makes the rising through the Military Revolutionary Committee and forms the Council of People’s Commissars.

def.q: The Bolsheviki proposed immediate proletarian insurrection, and seizure of the reins of Government, in order to hasten the coming of Socialism by forcibly taking over industry, land, natural resources and financial institutions.

also.q: This party expresses the desires chiefly of the factory workers, but also of a large section of the poor peasants.

bg.en: From April 1917 Lenin’s Bolsheviks called for “All power to the Soviets”, for peace and for land. They won the Petrograd and Moscow Soviets in September, prepared the rising through the Petrograd Soviet’s Military Revolutionary Committee, and on 8 November formed the Council of People’s Commissars. In March 1918 the party renamed itself the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks).

pic.lic: Public domain: a typographic cover too simple to be protected, published in 1917 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-ineligible}}, {{PD-old-80-1923}}, {{PD-old-80-expired}}, {{PD-old-X-expired}}, {{PD-trivial}})
pic.cap: The pamphlet Reed bought at the corner of the Nevsky, “Will the Bolsheviki be Able to Hold the Power?”, as he gives its title: the cover of the first edition (Petrograd: Priboi, 1917).

factions.name: Novaya Zhizn group (United Social Democrats Internationalists)
factions.sum: Gorky’s paper and its circle: they condemn the rising, yet stay in the Congress and plead for a socialist coalition.

def.q: Also called the Novaya Zhizn (New Life) group, from the name of the very influential newspaper which was its organ.

also.q: Opposed the Bolshevik tactics, but remained in the Soviet Government.

bg.en: Novaya Zhizn (“New Life”), the daily Maxim Gorky founded in Petrograd in April 1917 with Nikolai Sukhanov and others, attacked both the coalition government and the Bolsheviks; in its columns Gorky called the rising a reckless experiment on the Russian people. The Soviet government closed it in July 1918.

factions.name: Yedinstvo
factions.sum: Plekhanov’s following: for the war and against the rising.

def.q: A very small and dwindling group, composed almost entirely of the personal following of Plekhanov, one of the pioneers of the Russian Social Democratic movement in the 80’s, and its greatest theoretician.

bg.en: Georgi Plekhanov, who brought Marxism to Russia in the 1880s, came home from exile in 1917; his group, named after its paper Yedinstvo (“Unity”), backed the war to victory and the Provisional Government, and condemned the October rising. Plekhanov died in Finland in May 1918.

factions.name: The Bund (Jewish Social Democrats)
factions.sum: The Jewish socialist workers’ party; it sides with the Mensheviki and walks out of the Congress with them.

def.q: Then came Abramovitch, for the Bund, the organ of the Jewish Social Democrats

bg.en: The General Jewish Labour Bund of Lithuania, Poland and Russia, founded in Vilna in 1897, organised Jewish workers and stood for their national-cultural autonomy within a socialist Russia. In 1917 it sided with the Mensheviks, and its leaders, among them Mark Liber and Raphael Abramovitch, were also Menshevik leaders.

factions.name: Socialist Revolutionaries (SRs)
factions.sum: Russia’s largest party, the peasants’ party: Kerensky and Avksentiev are of it; it leads the Committee for Salvation and the yunker rising.

def.q: Originally the revolutionary party of the peasants, the party of the Fighting Organisations—the Terrorists.

also.q: They finally came to represent the wealthier peasants, the intellectuals, and the politically uneducated populations of remote rural districts.

bg.en: Founded in 1902 as heirs of the nineteenth-century Populists, the SRs wanted the land for those who work it, and their Combat Organisation assassinated ministers. In 1917 they were Russia’s largest party: Kerensky and Viktor Chernov sat in the Provisional Government, and in the elections to the Constituent Assembly, held in late November 1917, the SRs won the most votes.

pic.lic: Public domain: published in the United States more than 95 years ago; its author died long enough ago for it to be out of copyright (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-1923}}, {{PD-old}})
pic.cap: The leaders of the Socialist Revolutionaries at the party’s Third Congress, in Moscow in June 1917, under the banner “Land and Liberty. Party of Socialist Revolutionaries”: seated from the left Boris Kamkov, Nikolai Rusanov, Viktor Chernov, Maria Spiridonova, Mark Natanson and Vadim Rudnev, with Nikolai Avksentiev standing behind Rudnev. Left and right of the party sit side by side, months before the split.

factions.name: Left Socialist Revolutionaries
factions.sum: The SRs’ left wing: they stay in the Congress, back the Soviet power, win the Peasants’ Congress, and join the Council of People’s Commissars.

def.q: Although theoretically sharing the Bolshevik programme of dictatorship of the working-class, at first were reluctant to follow the ruthless Bolshevik tactics.

also.q: which became the great peasant party supporting the Soviet Government, standing for confiscation without compensation of the great landed estates, and their disposition by the peasants themselves.

bg.en: The SR left, led by Maria Spiridonova, Boris Kamkov and Mark Natanson, stayed in the Second Congress when the rest of the party walked out, was expelled by the SRs and founded its own party in December 1917. Its members joined the Council of People’s Commissars that month, Andrei Kolegaev as Commissar of Agriculture, and left it in March 1918 over the peace of Brest-Litovsk; their rising in Moscow in July 1918 ended the alliance with the Bolsheviks.

pic.lic: Public domain: published in the United States more than 95 years ago; its author died long enough ago for it to be out of copyright (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-1923}}, {{PD-old}})
pic.cap: The leaders of the Socialist Revolutionaries at the party’s Third Congress, in Moscow in June 1917, under the banner “Land and Liberty. Party of Socialist Revolutionaries”: seated from the left Boris Kamkov, Nikolai Rusanov, Viktor Chernov, Maria Spiridonova, Mark Natanson and Vadim Rudnev, with Nikolai Avksentiev standing behind Rudnev. Left and right of the party sit side by side, months before the split.

factions.name: Maximalists
factions.sum: A handful of peasant anarchists on the Soviet side.

def.q: An off-shoot of the Socialist Revolutionary party in the Revolution of 1905, when it was a powerful peasant movement, demanding the immediate application of the maximum Socialist programme.

bg.en: The Union of SR Maximalists broke away from the SRs in 1904–1906, demanding that the land and the factories be socialised at once, and practised expropriation and terror. In 1917 the little group supported the Soviet seizure of power.

factions.name: Soviets
factions.sum: The councils of workers’, soldiers’ and peasants’ deputies, in whose name the rising is made: “All Power to the Soviets!”

def.q: The word soviet means “council.”

also.q: the term Soviet has come to be associated with a certain type of parliament elected by members of working-class economic organisations—the Soviet of Workers’, of Soldiers’, or of Peasants’ Deputies.

bg.en: Workers’ councils first appeared in the revolution of 1905, when Trotsky chaired the St Petersburg Soviet. Revived in February 1917, they shared power with the Provisional Government, the “dual power”, until the Second All-Russian Congress of Soviets declared itself the government on 7–8 November.

factions.name: Petrograd Soviet
factions.ru: Петроградский Совет рабочих и солдатских депутатов
factions.sum: The capital’s council of workers’ and soldiers’ deputies, Bolshevik since September, with Trotzky in the chair: its Military Revolutionary Committee makes the rising.

def.q: On the 29th, in open session of the Petrograd Soviet, Trotzky proposed that the Soviet formally sanction the Military Revolutionary Committee.

bg.en: Formed on 12 March 1917 in the Tauride Palace by workers’ and soldiers’ deputies, it ran the city alongside the Provisional Government. It passed to the Bolsheviks in September 1917, when Trotsky became its chairman, and in October it set up the Military Revolutionary Committee that made the rising. It sat at Smolny.

pic.lic: Public domain: published in A. R. Williams, Through the Russian Revolution (New York, 1921) (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-US}})
pic.cap: Soldiers’ and workers’ deputies packed into a session of the Petrograd Soviet. Williams does not say which hall or when, so it may be the Tauride Palace before the Soviet moved to Smolny.
pic.by: Unknown; printed by A. R. Williams

factions.name: Second All-Russian Congress of Soviets
factions.sum: The congress that opens at Smolny on the night of the rising; after the Mensheviki and SRs walk out it takes power, decrees peace and land, and names the Council of People’s Commissars.

def.q: It was 10.40 P. M. Dan, a mild-faced, baldish figure in a shapeless military surgeon’s uniform, was ringing the bell.

bg.en: It opened in the great hall of Smolny late on 7 November with the Bolsheviks the largest group and the Left SRs their allies. Through the night the Mensheviks, the SRs and the Bund walked out; the rest proclaimed the power of the Soviets, and on 8 November passed the decrees on peace and on land, elected the Council of People’s Commissars and chose a new Central Executive Committee.

pic.lic: Public domain: a Soviet official document of 1917 whose author died in 1924 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-old}})
pic.cap: The Decree on Peace as printed for posting, “adopted unanimously” at the Congress session of 26 October, Old Style (8 November).
pic.by: V. I. Lenin, for the Congress of Soviets

factions.name: The old Tsay-ee-kah (Central Executive Committee)
factions.sum: The executive the first Congress of Soviets elected in June, moderate socialist: it tries to put off the Second Congress, then refuses to recognise it.

def.q: All-Russian Central Executive Committee of the Soviets of Workers’ and Soldiers’ Deputies. So called from the initials of its name.

bg.en: Elected by the First Congress of Soviets in June 1917 with a Menshevik and SR majority under Nikolay Chkheidze, it backed the coalition government and wanted the Second Congress postponed. Its leaders denied the Congress’s authority and joined the Committee for Salvation.

pic.t: Tcheidze, Tseretelli, Kameniev, Avksentiev and Schreider
pic.lic: Public domain: printed in Reed’s Ten Days That Shook the World (New York: Boni and Liveright, 1919) (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-1923}})
pic.cap: From the left, Tcheidze, Tseretelli, Kameniev, Avksentiev and Schreider: a plate in Reed’s 1919 edition. Tcheidze presided over the old Tsay-ee-kah and Tseretelli led the Mensheviki in the Soviets; Kameniev presided over the Second Congress; Avksentiev was president of the Peasants’ Soviets, and Schreider Mayor of Petrograd.

factions.name: The new Tsay-ee-kah
factions.sum: The executive the Second Congress elects, Bolshevik with the Left SRs: Kameniev chairs it, then Sverdlov; the peasants’ deputies join it later in November.

def.q: Kameniev was stripped of his powers as president of the Tsay-ee-kah, and Sverdlov elected in his place.

bg.en: Elected by the Second Congress of Soviets on 9 November 1917, with a Bolshevik majority and Left SRs, it was the Soviet state’s standing legislature between congresses. Lev Kamenev chaired it until 21 November, when Yakov Sverdlov replaced him; later that month it merged with the executive of the Peasants’ Congress.

factions.name: Executive Committee of the Peasants’ Soviets
factions.ru: Исполнительный комитет Всероссийского Совета крестьянских депутатов
factions.sum: The peasants’ executive, SR-led: it condemns the rising and joins the Committee for Salvation.
names: Executive Committee of the Peasants’ Soviets

def.q: with an Executive Committee of the All-Russian Peasants’ Soviets in the capital.

bg.en: Elected by the First All-Russian Congress of Peasants’ Deputies in May 1917, with an SR majority and Nikolai Avksentiev as its chairman, it stood with the Provisional Government and refused to recognise the Council of People’s Commissars.

pic.lic: Public domain: a postcard published in the Russian Empire before 1917 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-old}})
pic.cap: The Imperial School of Jurisprudence on the Fontanka, Fontanka 6, where the Peasants’ Soviet sat, on a postcard printed before 1917.

factions.name: Extraordinary Congress of Peasants’ Soviets
factions.ru: Чрезвычайный Всероссийский съезд Советов крестьянских депутатов
factions.sum: The peasant deputies who gather in Petrograd from late November: its Left SR majority, under Spiridonova, joins the Soviet power, and its SR minority walks out.

def.q: The Soviets of Peasants’ Deputies did not join the other two until after the Bolshevik coup d’etat.

bg.en: The Extraordinary Congress of Peasants’ Deputies opened in Petrograd on 23 November 1917 and chose Maria Spiridonova to chair it; its Left SR majority agreed to merge with the workers’ and soldiers’ Central Executive Committee, and the Right SR minority left.

factions.name: Military Revolutionary Committee
factions.sum: The Petrograd Soviet’s committee that commands the garrison and the Red Guards, takes the city on 6–7 November, and holds it for the Soviets.

def.q: We ought,” he said, “to create our special organisation to march to battle, and if necessary to die….”

also.q: On the 29th, in open session of the Petrograd Soviet, Trotzky proposed that the Soviet formally sanction the Military Revolutionary Committee.

bg.en: Set up by the Petrograd Soviet in October 1917, formally to defend the capital, it was the general staff of the rising. Its chairman was the Left SR Pavel Lazimir, its work was run by Bolsheviks such as Nikolai Podvoisky and Vladimir Antonov-Ovseenko under Trotsky’s lead, and it sent commissars into every unit of the garrison. It governed the city for weeks after the rising.

pic.lic: Public domain: a Soviet official document of 1917 (PD-RU-exempt), printed in Reed’s book in 1919 (PD in the US)
pic.cap: Pass to Smolny Institute, issued by the Military Revolutionary Committee, giving me the right of entry at any time.

factions.name: Council of People’s Commissars
factions.sum: The Soviet government the Congress names on 8 November, with Lenin at its head.

def.q: The governmental power is vested in a collegium made up of the chairmen of these commissions, that is to say, the Council of People’s Commissars.

bg.en: The government elected by the Second Congress of Soviets on 8 November 1917: at first all Bolsheviks, with Lenin as chairman, Trotsky for foreign affairs, Lunacharsky for education, and Antonov-Ovseenko, Krylenko and Dybenko for the army and navy. The Left SRs joined it in December 1917.

pic.t: The order to send Reed’s despatch
pic.lic: Public domain: a Soviet official document of 1917 (PD-RU-exempt), printed in Reed’s book in 1919 (PD in the US)
pic.cap: Order given me at Staff headquarters by command of the Council of People’s Commissars, to transmit the first despatch out of Perograd after the November Revolution

factions.name: Factory-Shop Committees
factions.sum: The workers’ committees in the mills and works, behind the Bolsheviki.

def.q: These were spontaneous organisations created in the factories by the workers in their attempt to control industry, taking advantage of the administrative break-down incident upon the Revolution.

bg.en: Elected in the works from March 1917, the factory committees pressed for workers’ control of production and were Bolshevik strongholds before the Soviets were. The Soviet decree on workers’ control of 27 November 1917 gave them legal powers.

factions.name: Trade Unions
factions.sum: Millions of workers in industrial unions, divided over the rising.

def.q: Although mostly industrial in form, the Russian labour unions were still called Trade Unions, and at the time of the Bolshevik Revolution had from three to four million members.

bg.en: The unions’ All-Russian Central Council was set up at a conference in June 1917. In November the unions were split over the Soviet power: the metalworkers backed it, the printers and the railwaymen’s leaders opposed it or demanded a coalition of all the socialist parties.

pic.lic: Public domain: a Soviet official document of 1917 (PD-RU-exempt), printed in Reed’s book in 1919 (PD in the US)
pic.cap: Appeal of the Petrograd Soviet, the Petrograd Council of Professional Unions, and the Petrograd Council of Factory Shop Committees, to the Workers of Petrograd, urging them to work hard and not to strike.

factions.name: Vikzhel (Railway Workers’ Union)
factions.sum: The railwaymen’s executive, neutral and powerful: it will not move troops for either side and demands a government of all the socialist parties.

def.q: All-Russian Central Committee of the Railway Workers’ Union. So called from the initials of its name.

also.q: In the name of the strongest organisation in Russia I demand the right to speak

bg.en: Led by Mensheviks and SRs, the railwaymen’s executive declared itself neutral after the rising and threatened a general rail strike unless a government of all the socialist parties was formed. It called the talks on such a coalition in November 1917; they failed within days.

factions.name: Army Committees
factions.sum: The soldiers’ elected committees, from the company up: the higher ones stand by the old leaders, the lower ones by the Soviets.

def.q: The Army Committees were formed by the soldiers at the front to combat the reactionary influence of the old regime officers.

bg.en: Soldiers’ committees spread through the army after the Petrograd Soviet’s Order No. 1 of 14 March 1917. Those elected in the spring were mostly SR and Menshevik at the higher levels, while by the autumn the regimental committees were turning Bolshevik; the Central Army Committee at Headquarters opposed the rising.

pic.lic: Public domain: a Soviet official document of 1917 (PD-RU-exempt), printed in Reed’s book in 1919 (PD in the US)
pic.cap: Announcement, posted on the walls of Petrograd, of the result of a meeting of representatives of the garrison regiments, called to consider the question of forming a new Government.

factions.name: Fleet Committees and Tsentroflot
factions.sum: The sailors’ committees: the Baltic sailors are the rising’s shock troops; the navy’s central committee, Tsentroflot, stands aside.

def.q: The corresponding organisations in the Navy.

also.q: Tsentroflot. “Centre-Fleet”—the Central Fleet Committee.

bg.en: Tsentrobalt, the Baltic Fleet’s central committee, chaired from April 1917 by the sailor Pavel Dybenko, refused to obey the Provisional Government in the autumn and sent the Kronstadt and Helsingfors sailors to Petrograd for the rising. Tsentroflot, the navy’s all-Russian committee, was pushed aside by the Bolsheviks after it.

pic.lic: Public domain: published in A. R. Williams, Through the Russian Revolution (New York, 1921) (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-US}})
pic.cap: Armed sailors in peakless caps with cap tallies, bayonets fixed, above a crowd of soldiers in papakhas. Williams printed it as “Revolutionary sailors”, with no place or date.
pic.by: Unknown; printed by A. R. Williams

factions.name: Provisional Government
factions.sum: Kerensky’s coalition cabinet, besieged in the Winter Palace on 7 November and arrested there that night.

def.q: When the Revolution broke out in March, 1917, the Cadets formed the first Provisional Government.

bg.en: Formed by leaders of the Duma on 15 March 1917, after the Tsar abdicated, under Prince Lvov and from July under Kerensky. It governed in coalition with the moderate socialists from May, kept Russia in the war, and put off the land question and the Constituent Assembly. Its last ministers were arrested in the Winter Palace in the early hours of 8 November.

pic.lic: Public domain: published in The Birth of the Russian Democracy (New York, 1918) (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-old}})
pic.cap: “The Last Provisional Cabinet”: Kerensky’s seventeen ministers of 8 October to 7 November 1917, numbered, with Kerensky (1), Tereshchenko (2), Kishkin (6), Konovalov (7), Prokopovich (9) and General Verkhovsky (13) among them; a page of The Birth of the Russian Democracy, New York, 1918.
pic.by: Unknown; printed in The Birth of the Russian Democracy

factions.name: Council of the Republic (the Pre-Parliament)
factions.sum: The consultative parliament in the Mariinsky Palace, dispersed by sailors on 7 November.

def.q: a sort of consultative Parliament, without any legislative power, called the Provisional Council of the Russian Republic.

bg.en: Set up by the Democratic Conference and opened on 20 October 1917 in the Mariinsky Palace, with Nikolai Avksentiev as its president; the Bolsheviks walked out on its first day. Soldiers and sailors of the Military Revolutionary Committee dispersed it on 7 November.

pic.t: The Council of the Republic in session
pic.lic: Public domain: printed in Reed’s Ten Days That Shook the World (New York: Boni and Liveright, 1919) (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-1923}})
pic.cap: The Council of the Russian Republic in session in the hall of the former Imperial Council of State, at the Marinsky Palace: a plate in Reed’s 1919 edition. Martov is speaking and Avksentiev presides; the picture is taken from the Bolshevik benches, empty since they walked out on the first day.

factions.name: City Duma
factions.sum: Petrograd’s elected town council, under the SR mayor Schreider: the heart of the resistance in the first days, where the Committee for Salvation is born.

def.q: The City Duma referred to in this book was the reorganised Municipal Council, often called “Municipal Self-Government.”

bg.en: Elected by universal suffrage in August 1917, with the SRs the largest party, the Petrograd City Duma chose Grigory Schreider as mayor. After the rising it became a centre of resistance to the Soviet power, and the Council of People’s Commissars dissolved it at the end of November 1917.

pic.lic: Public domain: a photochrom published in the 1890s (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-old}})
pic.cap: The City Duma and its clock tower on the Nevsky, in a photochrom of 1896–97. The colours are the printer’s.

factions.name: Committee for Salvation of Country and Revolution
factions.sum: The coalition of everyone against the rising, formed in the City Duma on its first night; it plans the yunker rising of 11 November.

def.q: the Committee for Salvation was formed—that Committee which was to develop into the most powerful enemy of the Bolsheviki

bg.en: Founded in the City Duma on the night of 7–8 November 1917 by the Duma, the old Central Executive Committee, the Peasants’ Executive, the Mensheviks, the SRs and others who had left the Congress of Soviets. It called for resistance, organised the rising of the yunkers on 11 November, and broke up after its failure.

factions.name: Union of Unions
factions.sum: The professional men’s federation; in 1917 it backs the officials’ strike against the Soviets.

def.q: In 1905 the Union of Unions acted with the revolutionary democracy; in 1917, however, the Union of Unions opposed the Bolshevik uprising, and united the Government employees who went on strike against the authority of the Soviets.

bg.en: Formed in May 1905 by the new unions of lawyers, doctors, engineers, teachers and other professions, with Pavel Miliukov as its chairman, it backed the general strike of October 1905.

factions.name: Zemstvos
factions.sum: The county councils of the countryside.

def.q: May be roughly translated “county councils.”

bg.en: The elected rural self-government created by Alexander II’s reform of 1864. In the war their All-Russian Union, under Prince Georgy Lvov, ran hospitals and supplies for the army, and Lvov became the first head of the Provisional Government.

factions.name: Cooperatives
factions.sum: The consumers’ societies, led by moderate socialists, against the rising.

def.q: These were the workers’ and peasants’ Consumers’ Cooperative societies, which had several million members all over Russia before the Revolution.

bg.en: Russia’s consumer, credit and producer cooperatives grew fast in the war and the revolution, with millions of members; their leaders, many of them Popular Socialists like Nikolai Tchaikovsky, sat in the Pre-Parliament and opposed the October rising.

factions.name: Peasants’ Union
factions.sum: The better-off peasants’ organisation, against the Peasants’ Soviets.

def.q: In 1917, however, it had become the political expression of the more prosperous peasants, to fight the growing power and revolutionary aims of the Soviets of Peasants’ Deputies.

bg.en: The All-Russian Peasant Union was founded at a congress in Moscow in the summer of 1905 and demanded the land for those who work it and a constituent assembly. Revived in 1917, it was soon overtaken by the Soviets of Peasants’ Deputies.

factions.name: Red Guards
factions.sum: The armed workers of the factories: with the soldiers and sailors, they take the city and storm the Winter Palace.

def.q: The armed factory workers of Russia.

also.q: At every great crisis in the Revolution the Red Guards appeared on the streets, untrained and undisciplined, but full of Revolutionary zeal.

bg.en: Workers’ militias formed in the factories after February 1917 and armed during General Kornilov’s attempt in August; by October Petrograd’s Red Guard numbered some twenty thousand men. They became the core of the Red Army, founded in 1918.

pic.t: The Red Guard of the Vulkan works
pic.lic: Public domain: its photographer, Viktor Bulla, died in 1938 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-old}})
pic.cap: The Red Guard of the Vulkan works under its banner, with a Maxim and a Colt machine gun.

factions.name: Stavka (General Headquarters)
factions.sum: The army’s high command at Moghilev, far behind the front: after Kerensky flees it is the last centre of the old army, until Krylenko takes it in December.

def.q: Moghilev (General Staff Headquarters).

bg.en: The Stavka, the headquarters of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief, stood at Moghilev from 1915. After the rising General Dukhonin, as acting Commander-in-Chief, refused the Soviet government’s order to open armistice talks; on 3 December 1917 Krylenko’s men took the Stavka and Dukhonin was killed.

factions.name: Yunkers (officer cadets)
factions.sum: The cadets of the military schools, the Government’s most dependable troops: they hold the Winter Palace on 7 November and rise against the Soviets on 11 November.

def.q: The yunkers of the Officers’ Schools of Pavlovsk, Tsarskoye Selo and Peterhof ordered by the Government to be ready to come to Petrograd.

also.q: In the Military Schools are retained only the arms necessary for instruction; all others are surrendered by the yunkers.

bg.en: Yunkers were the cadets of Russia’s military schools, many of them sons of educated and propertied families. They were the Provisional Government’s most dependable troops: they defended the Winter Palace on 7 November and, on 11 November, rose against the Soviets in Petrograd at the call of the Committee for Salvation; many were killed when the Vladimir school was stormed.

pic.lic: Public domain: a postcard published in the Russian Empire before 1917 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-RusEmpire}})
pic.cap: The St Petersburg Infantry Junker School on an old postcard. Renamed the Vladimir Military School in 1910, it is very probably the building the Red Guards stormed on 11 November.

factions.name: Cossacks
factions.sum: The cavalry of the Don and other borderlands: neutral in Petrograd, against the Soviets under Krasnov at Pulkovo and under Kaledin on the Don.

def.q: Now in the background of Russian politics began to form the vague outlines of a sinister power—the Cossacks.

bg.en: The Cossacks were the military estates of the Don, the Kuban and other borderlands, who served as cavalry in return for land and self-government. In November 1917 the three Cossack regiments in Petrograd stayed neutral; General Krasnov’s Cossacks marched on the capital for Kerensky and were turned back at Pulkovo, and Ataman Kaledin raised the Don against the Soviets.

pic.lic: Public domain: copyright expired (Australian War Memorial, EN0261)
pic.cap: General Krasnov (in the middle, in the tall Cossack fur hat), by then Ataman of the Don Cossacks, meets officers of the Allied Mission outside the cathedral at Novocherkassk, the Don’s capital, in December 1918, a year after he led Kerensky’s Cossacks on Petrograd.

factions.name: Death Battalions and the Women’s Battalion
factions.sum: Volunteer shock units; women of the Petrograd battalion are among the Winter Palace’s defenders.

def.q: The Women’s Battalion is known to the world as the Death Battalion, but there were many Death Battalions composed of men.

bg.en: Volunteer shock units raised in 1917 to stiffen the army by example. Maria Bochkareva’s 1st Russian Women’s Battalion of Death fought at the front in July 1917; a company of the 1st Petrograd Women’s Battalion was in the Winter Palace on 7 November.

pic.lic: Public domain: published in E. A. Ross, The Russian Bolshevik Revolution (New York, 1921) (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-RusEmpire}})
pic.cap: Women soldiers in greatcoats and fur hats drawn up on Palace Square before the arch of the General Staff. Ross printed it in 1921 as the women’s Battalion of Death, without a date.
pic.by: Unknown; printed by E. A. Ross

factions.name: White Guards
factions.sum: Middle-class volunteers who take up arms for the old order.

def.q: Bourgeois volunteers, who emerged in the last stages of the Revolution, to defend private property from the Bolshevik attempt to abolish it.

bg.en: The name passed to the anti-Bolshevik armies of the Civil War of 1918–1920, the Whites.

factions.name: Tekhintsi and the “Savage Division”
factions.sum: Kornilov’s own horsemen.

def.q: The so-called “Savage Division” in the army, made up of Mohametan tribesmen from Central Asia, and personally devoted to General Kornilov.

bg.en: Kornilov’s personal guard was the Tekke regiment of Turkmen horsemen from Transcaspia; the “Savage Division”, the Caucasian Native Cavalry Division of volunteers from the North Caucasus, was part of the force he sent against Petrograd in August 1917, whose men were talked out of marching on by Soviet agitators.

factions.name: Union of Officers
factions.sum: The officers’ league against the soldiers’ committees.

def.q: An organisation formed among the reactionary officers in the army to combat politically the growing power of the Army Committees.

bg.en: The Union of Officers of the Army and Navy, founded at Headquarters in May 1917, backed General Kornilov’s attempt in August 1917 and was suppressed after it failed.

factions.name: Knights of St. George
factions.sum: The holders of the Cross of St. George, for the war.

def.q: The Cross of St. George was awarded for distinguished action in battle.

bg.en: The Cross of St George, the army’s highest award for bravery, was given to soldiers and officers; in 1917 its holders formed a union that backed the war and a firm government.

people.name: Raphael Abramovitch
people.role: Bund leader

def.q: Then came Abramovitch, for the Bund, the organ of the Jewish Social Democrats—his eyes snapping behind thick glasses, trembling with rage.

bio.en: Born Rafail Rein, a leader of the Bund and of the Mensheviks, he walked the Bund out of the Second Congress of Soviets. He left Soviet Russia in 1920, led the Mensheviks abroad with Dan and Martov, and died in New York in 1963.

pic.lic: Public domain: published anonymously more than 95 years ago (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-anon-expired}})

people.name: Vladimir Antonov-Ovseenko
people.role: Secretary of the Military Revolutionary Committee; led the taking of the Winter Palace

def.q: a certain Avseenko, called Antonov, mathematician and chess-player; he was drawing careful plans for the seizure of the capital.

bio.en: A former army officer and a Menshevik before he joined the Bolsheviks in 1917, he directed the taking of the Winter Palace and arrested the ministers there. One of the three commissars for military and naval affairs, he commanded Red armies in Ukraine in the Civil War and was shot in Stalin’s purges in 1938.

pic.lic: Public domain: published in A. R. Williams, Through the Russian Revolution (New York, 1921) (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-Scan}}, {{PD-old-100}})
pic.by: Unknown; printed by A. R. Williams

people.name: Boris Avilov
people.role: Social Democrat of the Novaya Zhizn group

def.q: Avilov, with his young, intelligent face, looking out of place in his smart frock-coat.

bio.en: A Marxist who broke with the Bolsheviks in 1917, he founded the United Social Democrat Internationalists with Vladimir Bazarov and others, a small group that tried to bring the Menshevik Internationalists and the moderate Bolsheviks together; at the Second Congress of Soviets he argued for a government of all the socialist parties.

people.name: Nikolai Avksentiev
people.role: SR leader; president of the Peasants’ Soviets and of the Council of the Republic

def.q: Avksentiev, the lean, red-bearded president of the Peasants’ Soviets

bio.en: A right-wing SR, he was minister of the interior in the summer of 1917 and then president of the Council of the Republic. After the rising he led the Committee for Salvation; in the autumn of 1918 he chaired the anti-Bolshevik Directory at Omsk until Admiral Kolchak’s coup, and he died in exile in New York in 1943.

pic.lic: Public domain: printed in Reed’s Ten Days That Shook the World (New York: Boni and Liveright, 1919) (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-1923}})

people.name: Catherine Breshkovsky
people.role: “Babuschka”, the grandmother of the Russian revolution

bio.en: A noblewoman who went “to the people” in the 1870s, she spent decades in prison, hard labour and Siberian exile and was among the founders of the SRs. Hailed in 1917 as the grandmother of the revolution, she backed the Provisional Government and the war, left Russia in 1919 and died in Czechoslovakia in 1934.

pic.lic: Public domain: out of copyright in the United States, by a rule Commons does not name (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-US}})
pic.by: Published by Little, Brown and Co, Boston, 1918; photographer unknown

people.name: Fyodor Dan
people.role: Menshevik leader; opened the Second Congress

def.q: Dan, a mild-faced, baldish figure in a shapeless military surgeon’s uniform

bio.en: A doctor and Martov’s brother-in-law, he was a leader of the Menshevik majority in the Soviets in 1917 and of the old Central Executive Committee, and opened the Second Congress of Soviets from the chair. Expelled from Soviet Russia in 1922, he led the Mensheviks abroad and died in New York in 1947.

pic.lic: Public domain: its author died more than 70 years ago (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-old-70}})

people.name: Nikolai Dukhonin
people.role: Acting Commander-in-Chief at Moghilev

def.q: the Staff at Moghilev, where General Dukhonin had assumed command.

bio.en: Chief of staff at Headquarters in Moghilev, he became acting Commander-in-Chief when Kerensky fled. Ordered by the Council of People’s Commissars to open armistice talks with the Germans, he refused and was dismissed; on 3 December 1917, when Krylenko’s men took Headquarters, soldiers and sailors lynched him.

people.name: Pavel Dybenko
people.role: Chairman of the Baltic sailors’ committee; Commissar for the Navy

def.q: Dybenko, the giant bearded sailor with the placid face.

bio.en: A Baltic sailor of peasant stock, chairman of the Baltic Fleet’s central committee, Tsentrobalt, from April 1917, he brought the Kronstadt and Helsingfors sailors to the rising and became one of the three commissars for military and naval affairs. He married Alexandra Kollontai, commanded in the Civil War, and was shot in 1938.

pic.lic: Public domain: its author died long enough ago for it to be out of copyright (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-old}})

people.name: Maxim Gorky
people.role: Writer; publisher of Novaya Zhizn

def.q: except the personal following of Maxim Gorky, its leader.

bio.en: Born Alexei Peshkov in Nizhny Novgorod, the most famous Russian writer of his day and an old friend of Lenin’s, he used his paper Novaya Zhizn to denounce the rising and the terror that followed it. He left Russia in 1921, came back to Stalin’s Soviet Union in the 1930s, and died in 1936.

pic.lic: Public domain: its author died more than 70 years ago (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-old-auto-expired}})

people.name: Abram Gotz
people.role: SR leader in the old Tsay-ee-kah

def.q: Gotz, ringing the chairman’s bell: “Silence, or I’ll have you put out!”

bio.en: An SR terrorist sentenced to hard labour before the war, he led the SRs in the Petrograd Soviet and the old Central Executive Committee in 1917, and was a leader of the Committee for Salvation and of the yunker rising. Sentenced to death at the trial of the SRs in 1922 and reprieved, he died in a labour camp in 1940.

pic.lic: Public domain: its author died more than 70 years ago (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-old-70}})

people.name: Alexey Kaledin
people.role: Ataman of the Don Cossacks

def.q: Kaledin, ataman of the Don Cossacks, had been dismissed by the Provisional Government for his complicity in the Kornilov affair.

bio.en: A cavalry general elected ataman of the Don Cossacks in June 1917, he refused to recognise the Soviet government and made the Don the Whites’ first base; when his Cossacks would no longer fight, he shot himself in February 1918.

pic.lic: Public domain: published in Russia, its author dead or unknown before 1943 (Russian law); published in Russia before 1946, with no author named or the author dead before 1946 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-Russia-1996}}, {{PD-Russia-2008}})

people.name: Lev Kamenev
people.role: Bolshevik leader; first chairman of the new Tsay-ee-kah

def.q: Kameniev, a little man with a reddish pointed beard and Gallic gestures.

bio.en: With Zinoviev he opposed the rising in the Bolshevik Central Committee in October 1917 and said so in the press. He chaired the Second Congress of Soviets and its new executive, and resigned in November when his party refused a coalition with the other socialists. Stalin’s partner and then his victim, he was shot after the first Moscow show trial in 1936.

pic.lic: Public domain: a photograph taken in Norway more than 50 years ago, before 1969 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-Norway50}})

people.name: Boris Kamkov
people.role: Left SR leader

def.q: the Left Socialist Revolutionaries, led by Kamkov and Spiridonova

bio.en: With Spiridonova he led the Left SRs out of the old party in 1917 and into the alliance with the Bolsheviks, and then into the break with them over the peace of Brest-Litovsk in 1918. After years of prison and exile he was killed in the Great Purge in 1938.

pic.lic: Public domain: published in the Russian Empire before 1917; its author died more than 100 years ago; published anonymously more than 95 years ago (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-RusEmpire}}, {{PD-anon-1923}}, {{PD-anon-expired}}, {{PD-old-100}})

people.name: Vladimir Karelin
people.role: Left SR leader; People’s Commissar of State Properties

def.q: Karelin followed him—also young, fearless, whose sincerity no one doubted

bio.en: One of the founders of the Left SR party and a member of its central committee, he was People’s Commissar of State Properties in the Soviet government from December 1917 to March 1918, when the Left SRs left it over the peace of Brest-Litovsk.

pic.lic: Public domain: its author died long enough ago for it to be out of copyright (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-old}})

people.name: Alexander Kerensky
people.role: Minister-President of the Provisional Government

def.q: Kerensky was the leader of the Trudoviki in the Imperial Duma when the Revolution of March, 1917, broke out.

bio.en: A lawyer famous for political defences and the Trudovik leader in the Fourth Duma, he was the only socialist in the first Provisional Government, minister of war in the summer of 1917 and prime minister from July. He left the Winter Palace on 7 November to bring troops from the front, was beaten at Pulkovo, went into hiding and then into exile, and died in New York in 1970.

pic.lic: Public domain: its photographer, Karl Bulla, died in 1929 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-RusEmpire}})

people.name: Nikolai Kishkin
people.role: Cadet; given charge of order in Petrograd on 7 November

def.q: First came Kishkin, his face drawn and pale

bio.en: A Moscow doctor and a member of the Cadets’ central committee, minister of state relief in Kerensky’s last cabinet, he was given full powers to restore order in Petrograd on the day of the rising and was arrested in the Winter Palace that night. He later worked in the Soviet health service.

pic.lic: Public domain: published in the Russian Empire before 1917; its author died more than 100 years ago; published anonymously more than 95 years ago (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-RusEmpire}}, {{PD-anon-1923}}, {{PD-anon-expired}}, {{PD-old-100}})

people.name: Andrei Kolegaev
people.role: People’s Commissar of Agriculture

bio.en: A Left SR who argued for the alliance with the Bolsheviks, he was People’s Commissar of Agriculture from December 1917 until the Left SRs left the government in March 1918, and later joined the Bolsheviks.

people.name: Alexandra Kollontai
people.role: People’s Commissar of Social Welfare

def.q: Alexandra Kollontai, appointed the 13th of November Commissar of Public Welfare—the department of charities and public institutions—was welcomed with a strike of all but forty of the functionaries in the Ministry.

bio.en: A general’s daughter turned Marxist, she joined the Bolsheviks in 1915 and was the only woman in the first Soviet government, where she worked for the rights of women and mothers. From 1923 she was a Soviet diplomat, in Norway, Mexico and Sweden, among the first women ambassadors in the world.

pic.lic: Public domain: published anonymously more than 70 years ago (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-anon-70-EU}})

people.name: Alexander Konovalov
people.role: Industrialist; deputy prime minister in the last cabinet

def.q: Typical of the Group: Lianozov, Konovalov.

bio.en: A Moscow textile magnate and a leader of the Progressists in the Duma, he was minister of trade in 1917 and deputy prime minister in Kerensky’s last cabinet; he presided over the ministers in the Winter Palace after Kerensky left, and was arrested there. He died in exile in New York in 1949.

pic.lic: Public domain: its author died long enough ago for it to be out of copyright (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-old}})

people.name: Lavr Kornilov
people.role: Commander-in-Chief; led the August attempt on Petrograd

def.q: Kornilov, who introduced capital punishment for soldiers and Cossacks at the front.

bio.en: A Cossack’s son who rose to general, Commander-in-Chief from July 1917, he sent troops against Petrograd in August to put down the Soviets, failed and was arrested. He escaped to the Don in December, founded the Volunteer Army with General Alexeyev, and was killed by a shell outside Ekaterinodar in April 1918.

pic.lic: Public domain: published in Russia, its author dead or unknown before 1943 (Russian law) (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-Russia}})

people.name: Pyotr Krasnov
people.role: General; led Kerensky’s Cossacks against Petrograd

def.q: General Krasnov, who said, “You fought against Kornilov; now you are opposing Kerensky. I’ll have you all shot!”

bio.en: A Don Cossack general and novelist, he commanded the Third Cavalry Corps that Kerensky led on Petrograd; beaten at Pulkovo, he was let go on his word of honour and went to the Don, where he was ataman in 1918. In exile he sided with Nazi Germany, was handed over to the Soviets in 1945 and was hanged in Moscow in 1947.

pic.lic: Public domain: its author died more than 100 years ago (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-old-100-expired}})

people.name: Nikolai Krylenko
people.role: Commissar for military affairs; then Commander-in-Chief

def.q: Krylenko, the squat, wide-faced soldier, always smiling, with his violent gestures and tumbling speech

bio.en: A Bolshevik ensign and agitator at the front, he became one of the three commissars for military affairs and, on 22 November 1917, Supreme Commander-in-Chief in place of General Dukhonin. Later the Soviet chief prosecutor and People’s Commissar for Justice, he was shot in the Great Purge in 1938.

pic.lic: Public domain: published in 1918 (US) (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-1923}}, {{PD-US-expired}})

people.name: Vladimir Lenin
people.role: Leader of the Bolsheviki; chairman of the Council of People’s Commissars

def.q: A short, stocky figure, with a big head set down in his shoulders, bald and bulging.

bio.en: Born Vladimir Ulyanov in Simbirsk; his elder brother was hanged in 1887 for a plot against Alexander III. A Marxist lawyer and writer, he founded the Bolshevik wing in 1903 and spent most of the years until 1917 in exile. Back in Petrograd in April 1917, he called for the Soviets to take power; hiding after July, he pressed his party into the rising, and on 8 November became head of the Soviet government, which he led until his death in 1924.

pic.lic: Public domain: its photographer, Dmitry Leshchenko, died in 1937 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-Russia}})

people.name: Stepan Lianozov
people.role: Oil magnate

bio.en: An oil industrialist of Armenian descent whose firm worked the Baku fields, called the “Russian Rockefeller”, he left Russia after the rising and in 1919 headed the anti-Bolshevik North-Western Government in Estonia.

people.name: Mikhail Liber
people.role: Menshevik and Bund leader

def.q: the long-faced, cruel-tongued Lieber

bio.en: Born Mikhail Goldman, a leader of the Bund and of the Menshevik defencists, he sat in the presidium of the Soviets’ old Central Executive Committee in 1917, where the Bolsheviks mocked him and Dan together as the “Lieber-Dans”. He was shot in 1937.

pic.lic: Public domain: published in the Russian Empire before 1917 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-RusEmpire}})

people.name: Anatoly Lunacharsky
people.role: People’s Commissar of Education

def.q: Lunatcharsky, a slight, student-like figure with the sensitive face of an artist

bio.en: A critic and playwright, he came over to the Bolsheviks with Trotsky’s group in the summer of 1917. As People’s Commissar of Education from November 1917 to 1929 he worked to open the schools, theatres and museums to the people and to keep the intelligentsia on the Soviet side. He died in France in 1933 on his way to take up the post of ambassador to Spain.

pic.lic: Public domain: its author died long enough ago for it to be out of copyright (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-old}})

people.name: Julius Martov
people.role: Leader of the Menshevik Internationalists

def.q: Martov, constantly interrupted: “The Internationalists are not opposed to the transmission of power to the democracy, but they disapprove of the methods of the Bolsheviki.

bio.en: Born Yuly Tsederbaum in Constantinople, Lenin’s partner in founding the Marxist paper Iskra and then his opponent at the split of 1903, he led the Mensheviks’ internationalist wing against the war. He opposed the Bolshevik dictatorship from inside the Soviets until he left Russia in 1920, and died in Germany in 1923.

pic.lic: Public domain: its photographer, Yakov Steinberg, died in 1942 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-Russia-expired}})

people.name: Pavel Miliukov
people.role: Leader of the Cadets

def.q: Paul Miliukov, leader of the Cadets, made a brilliant, bitter speech

bio.en: A historian and the founder and leader of the Cadets, he was foreign minister in the first Provisional Government until his note promising to fight the war to victory brought crowds into the streets and forced him out in May 1917. He opposed the Soviets from the Council of the Republic and in the Civil War, and died in France in 1943.

pic.lic: Public domain: its author died long enough ago for it to be out of copyright (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-old}})

people.name: Sofia Panina
people.role: Cadet; deputy minister in 1917

def.q: the former Minister, Countess Panina, had gone off with all the funds, which she refused to surrender except on the order of the Constituent Assembly.

bio.en: A philanthropist who built a people’s house for the workers of Petrograd, she was the first woman in a Russian government, as deputy minister of state welfare and then of education in 1917. Tried by a revolutionary tribunal in December 1917 for keeping her ministry’s funds from the Soviets, she was let off lightly, left Russia in 1920 and died in New York in 1956.

pic.lic: Public domain: out of copyright in the United States, by a rule Commons does not name (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-US}})

people.name: Aleksey Peshekhonov
people.role: Popular Socialist; Minister of Food in 1917

bio.en: An economist and journalist and a founder of the Popular Socialists, he was minister of food in the coalition of 1917. Expelled from Soviet Russia with other intellectuals in 1922, he died in Riga in 1933.

people.name: Georgi Plekhanov
people.role: Founder of Russian Marxism; leader of Yedinstvo

def.q: Now an old man, Plekhanov was extremely patriotic, too conservative even for the Mensheviki.

bio.en: A Populist turned Marxist, he founded the first Russian Marxist group, the Emancipation of Labour, in Geneva in 1883 and taught a generation, Lenin among them. After 1903 he went with the Mensheviks; in 1917 he backed the war and condemned the October rising, and he died of tuberculosis in Finland in 1918.

pic.lic: Public domain: its author died more than 70 years ago (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-old-70}})

people.name: Nikolai Podvoisky
people.role: Head of the Bolshevik Military Organisation; planned the rising

def.q: Podvoisky, the thin, bearded civillian whose brain conceived the strategy of insurrection

bio.en: Head of the Bolshevik Military Organisation, which worked among the soldiers of the garrison, he sat on the Military Revolutionary Committee and directed the operations against the Winter Palace, then became the first People’s Commissar for Military and Naval Affairs. He survived the purges and died in 1948.

people.name: Sergei Prokopovich
people.role: Minister of Supplies

def.q: Prokopovitch, Minister of Supplies in the Provisional Government, arrested that morning and released.

bio.en: An economist and statistician, minister of trade and then of food in 1917, he was outside the Winter Palace when it fell and led the underground remnant of the Provisional Government for some weeks after. Expelled from Soviet Russia in 1922, he died in Geneva in 1955.

pic.lic: Public domain: its author died long enough ago for it to be out of copyright (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-old}})

people.name: David Riazanov
people.role: Bolshevik of the trade unions, on his party’s right

def.q: Riazanov, vice-president of the Trade Unions, looking black and biting his grey beard.

bio.en: A Marxist scholar who joined the Bolsheviks in 1917, he opposed a government of one party and pressed for a coalition of all the socialists. He founded the Marx–Engels Institute in Moscow and edited the first complete works of Marx and Engels; arrested in 1931, he was shot in 1938.

pic.lic: Public domain: its author died more than 70 years ago (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-old-70}})

people.name: Mikhail Rodzianko
people.role: Chairman of the Imperial Duma

bio.en: A landowner and Octobrist, chairman of the State Duma from 1911, he helped bring about the Tsar’s abdication in March 1917. After the rising he joined the Whites in the South, and he died in exile in Yugoslavia in 1924.

pic.lic: Public domain: out of copyright in the United States, by a rule Commons does not name (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-US}})

people.name: Grigory Schreider
people.role: Mayor of Petrograd

def.q: white-bearded old Schreider, Mayor of Petrograd

bio.en: An economist and journalist and a member of the SRs, he was mayor of Petrograd in 1917; after the rising he led the City Duma’s resistance and its procession toward the Winter Palace, until the Soviet government dissolved the Duma at the end of November.

pic.lic: Public domain: printed in Reed’s Ten Days That Shook the World (New York: Boni and Liveright, 1919) (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-1923}})

people.name: Andrei Shingarev
people.role: Cadet; Minister of Agriculture, then of Finance, in 1917

def.q: Shingariov, Cadet, then demanded that all Municipal functionaries who had consented to be Commissars of the Military Revolutionary Committee be discharged from their position and indicted.

bio.en: A country doctor turned Cadet deputy, he was minister of agriculture and then of finance in 1917. Arrested in late November 1917 with other Cadet leaders, he was murdered with Fyodor Kokoshkin by sailors in a Petrograd hospital in January 1918.

pic.lic: Public domain: published in the Russian Empire before 1917 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-RusEmpire}})

people.name: Vasily Shulgin
people.role: Monarchist deputy of the Duma

bio.en: A Kiev nationalist and monarchist, he was one of the two Duma deputies who received Nicholas II’s abdication at Pskov in March 1917, and a thinker of the White movement. Seized in Yugoslavia in 1944, he served twelve years in Soviet prisons and died in the Soviet Union in 1976, at ninety-eight.

pic.lic: Public domain: published in the Russian Empire before 1917 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-RusEmpire}})

people.name: Matvey Skobelev
people.role: Menshevik; Minister of Labour in 1917

def.q: The Soviets chose Skobeliev to speak for them and drew up a manifesto, the famous nakaz

bio.en: A Menshevik deputy of the Fourth Duma, he was Minister of Labour in the coalition governments of 1917 and, after the rising, helped to found the Committee for Salvation. He later went over to the Communists, worked in Soviet economic administration, and was shot in 1938.

pic.lic: Public domain: its author died long enough ago for it to be out of copyright (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-old}})

people.name: Maria Spiridonova
people.role: Leader of the Left SRs; chair of the Peasants’ Congress

def.q: Maria Spiridonova, slight, pale, with spectacles and hair drawn flatly down, and the air of a New England school-teacher, took the tribune—the most loved and the most powerful woman in all Russia.

bio.en: In 1906, at twenty-one, she shot a provincial official who had put down a peasant rising, and her account of her treatment after it made her famous; she spent eleven years in Siberia. Freed in 1917, she led the Left SRs, broke with the Bolsheviks over the peace of Brest-Litovsk and the grain requisitions, and spent the rest of her life in prison and exile until she was shot in 1941.

people.name: Yakov Sverdlov
people.role: Chairman of the new Tsay-ee-kah from 21 November

def.q: Kameniev was stripped of his powers as president of the Tsay-ee-kah, and Sverdlov elected in his place.

bio.en: The Bolsheviks’ organiser, who ran the party’s secretariat in 1917, he succeeded Kamenev as chairman of the Central Executive Committee in November 1917, which made him the Soviet head of state, until he died in the influenza epidemic in March 1919.

people.name: Nikolai Tchaikovsky
people.role: Veteran Populist; leader of the Cooperatives

bio.en: A Populist of the 1870s whose circle, the Chaikovtsy, sent students “to the people”, he lived for decades in exile; in 1917 he led the Popular Socialists and the Cooperative movement. In 1918–1919 he headed the anti-Bolshevik government at Archangel under Allied protection, and died in London in 1926.

people.name: Viktor Chernov
people.role: SR founder and leader; Minister of Agriculture in 1917

def.q: Tchernov’s wide face, with the small eyes, waving hair and greyish beard, became red with wrath

bio.en: The SRs’ chief theorist and one of the founders of the party, he was minister of agriculture in the coalition from May to August 1917. Elected president of the Constituent Assembly, he chaired its only session on 18 January 1918 before the Bolsheviks dispersed it, and he died in exile in New York in 1952.

people.name: Mikhail Tereshchenko
people.role: Foreign Minister of the Provisional Government

def.q: Terestchenko was next, glancing sharply around; he stared at us with cold fixity

bio.en: A sugar millionaire from Kiev and of no party, he was minister of finance and, from May 1917, foreign minister; he was arrested with the others in the Winter Palace. He got away abroad in 1918 and died in Monaco in 1956.

people.name: Leon Trotsky
people.role: Chairman of the Petrograd Soviet; led the rising; Commissar for Foreign Affairs

def.q: His thin, pointed face was positively Mephistophelian in its expression of malicious irony.

bio.en: Born Lev Bronstein near Kherson, he chaired the St Petersburg Soviet in 1905 and stood between the factions for years. He joined the Bolsheviks in the summer of 1917, became chairman of the Petrograd Soviet in October and led the rising through its Military Revolutionary Committee. He founded the Red Army in 1918, lost the struggle for power to Stalin after Lenin’s death, was expelled from the Soviet Union in 1929 and was murdered in Mexico in 1940 on Stalin’s orders.

people.name: Irakli Tsereteli
people.role: Menshevik leader; minister in 1917

def.q: the high-souled Tseretelli, also mortally stricken, who, nevertheless, would return and pour out his beautiful eloquence for a lost cause.

bio.en: A Georgian Social Democrat sent to hard labour after the Second Duma, he came back from Siberia in 1917 to lead the Mensheviks in the Soviet and was minister of posts and telegraphs, then of the interior, in the coalition. He later served independent Menshevik Georgia and died in exile in New York in 1959.

people.name: Moisei Uritsky
people.role: Member of the Military Revolutionary Committee

bio.en: A member of the Bolshevik Central Committee and of the Military Revolutionary Committee in 1917, he headed the Petrograd Cheka in 1918 and was assassinated that August, on the day of the attempt on Lenin’s life; the two attacks opened the Red Terror.

people.name: Alexander Verkhovsky
people.role: Minister of War until early November

def.q: General Verkhovsky, Minister of War, insisted that only a new, voluntary, democratic discipline, based on cooperation with the soldiers’ and sailors’ Committees, could save the army and navy.

bio.en: A young general, minister of war from September 1917, he told the government in October that the army could not go on fighting and urged peace, and was sent on leave days before the rising. He later served in the Red Army and was shot in 1938.

people.name: Maxim Vinaver
people.role: Cadet leader

bio.en: A Petersburg lawyer, a founder of the Cadet party and a leader of the struggle for Jewish civil rights, he went south after the rising, served the regional government of the Crimea in 1918–1919, and died in exile in France in 1926.

people.name: V. Volodarsky
people.role: Bolshevik orator of the Petrograd Soviet

def.q: Volodarsky, a tall, pale youth with glasses and a bad complexion, was more definite.

bio.en: Born Moisei Goldstein, he came back from emigration in America in 1917 and was one of the Bolsheviks’ best-known orators in Petrograd; the city’s commissar for press and propaganda, he was shot dead by an SR in June 1918.

people.name: Grigory Zinoviev
people.role: Bolshevik leader; Lenin’s companion in exile

def.q: Lenin and Zinoviev went into hiding, fugitives from justice

bio.en: Lenin’s closest companion in the years of exile, he hid with him after the July Days, opposed the rising with Kamenev, and in December 1917 became chairman of the Petrograd Soviet. He headed the Communist International from 1919; condemned with Kamenev, he was shot in 1936.
